title: Data from Utah's Sandbox Shows Extraordinary Promise, Refutes Fears of Harm
pub: IAALS — University of Denver (Unlocking Legal Regulation project)
author: IAALS (Institute for the Advancement of the American Legal System)

dom.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: IAALS rejects the cluster’s cautious assessment of access and complaint evidence. It treats Utah’s early supervised-sandbox data as demonstrating real consumer access and as refuting harm concerns, rather than merely showing diverse proposed models and low recorded complaint incidence whose broader benefits remain unproven.
qs: Despite trepidation from some in the legal community around the idea of nonlawyers providing legal services, with harm to consumers cited as one of the biggest risks, newly released data from the sandbox proves those fears unfounded—and that, in fact, the opposite is true.

### The Evaluation  Although it’s been just over a year, it’s undeniable that the sandbox is providing thousands of consumers with a variety of legal services, creating new jobs for lawyers and other types of professionals, and equipping courts, policymakers, and other justice system stakeholders with incredibly valuable data.

st.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk
st.an: IAALS supports conditional, court-supervised experimentation to expand access while managing consumer risk. It presents early service and complaint data more confidently than the cluster synthesis permits, but acknowledges that substantially more evidence is needed; this is an evidentiary overclaim rather than rejection of the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: The Office of Legal Services Innovation utilizes a risk-based regulation framework when assessing entities for recommendation to the court, considering both the likelihood of harm—as well as the degree of harm—that applicants pose to consumers.

We still have a long way to go and a lot of data to collect, but what we’ve seen so far does suggest that re-regulation has the potential to meaningfully increase access to justice and, importantly, the data shows that these kinds of innovations can be done safely.

mo.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier
Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production

kp.k: Utah permits supervised experimentation with nontraditional legal services
kp.d: The September 15, 2021 article describes Utah's regulatory sandbox, established the previous August, as the first state initiative allowing lawyers and other professionals to deliver nontraditional legal services under state supreme court supervision. The authors attribute the emergence of new businesses and collaborations to these regulatory reforms.
qs: providing a space for lawyers and other professionals to deliver nontraditional legal services under the supervision of the state supreme court.
None of this would have been possible without the groundbreaking reforms passed last fall.

kp.k: Risk-based oversight adapts as provider data accumulates
kp.d: Reporting data through July 2021, the article identifies 30 court-approved entities: four low risk, 12 low–moderate risk, 13 moderate risk, and one high risk. The Office of Legal Services Innovation assesses both likelihood and degree of consumer harm when recommending applicants and continually adjusts assessments as data arrives.
qs: So far, 30 entities have been approved by the Utah Supreme Court—of these, four are categorized as low risk, 12 as low–moderate risk, 13 as moderate risk, and one as high risk.
These assessments will be continuously adjusted as the Office of Legal Services Innovation receives more data from the sandbox.

kp.k: Early service volumes span diverse consumer legal needs
kp.d: The reported activity comprised over 3,000 legal services sought by about 2,500 unduplicated clients. Service categories included end-of-life planning (19.6%), business matters (22.3%), and marriage and family (15.0%), alongside education, real estate, domestic violence, and immigration. The authors interpret these volumes as evidence of high demand.
qs: including end-of-life planning (19.6%); business-related matters such as intellectual property, contracts and warranties, and entity incorporation (22.3%); and marriage and family (15.0%).
The data also makes it clear that these services are in high demand—thus far, over 3,000 legal services have been sought from about 2,500 unduplicated clients.

kp.k: Software delivery operates with lawyer involvement
kp.d: The article reports over 550 services delivered through software with lawyer involvement and asserts that technology enables more efficient work. Its concrete examples concern software, document generation, chat-bots, and messaging, rather than a separately measured AI intervention.
qs: The ability to utilize technology, too, is making a substantial impact, with over 550 legal services delivered by software (with lawyer involvement).
Lawyers are partnering up with other professionals to create new types of businesses, and technology is enabling them to do their jobs more efficiently.

kp.k: Low complaint rates underpin authors' consumer-safety argument
kp.d: The article reports two harm-related complaints, one complaint per 1,000 services delivered, and one harm-related complaint per 1,500 services delivered. It quotes the monitoring report's assessment that entity responses were adequate for mitigation and interprets this as suggesting remediation or prevention plans. The authors characterize early data as refuting fears of consumer harm while acknowledging that more data remains to be collected.
qs: There have been a few complaints made to the Office of Legal Services Innovation, with two of those being harm-related.
At the current rate of legal needs being met, there’s been one complaint per 1,000 services delivered; one harm-related complaint for every 1,500 services delivered.
entity response to harm-related complaints has been adequate and acceptable as related to mitigation
newly released data from the sandbox proves those fears unfounded—and that, in fact, the opposite is true.

kp.k: Nonlawyer ownership supports new delivery and employment arrangements
kp.d: The authors illustrate regulatory flexibility through 1Law, which combines free and low-cost court-document assistance and related legal advice with chat-bots, instant messaging, and nonlawyer staff, and has more than 50% nonlawyer ownership. Bee Bankruptcy Law's owner applied to give a paralegal employee a 10% ownership interest. LawPal provides document generation for divorce, custody, eviction, and debt-related property seizure cases.
qs: provides free and low-cost legal services to assist clients in completing court documents, and also offers related legal advice using chat-bots, instant messaging, and nonlawyer staff.
And, the organization has more than 50% nonlawyer ownership—an impossibility under most states’ current regulatory framework.

Other participants in the sandbox include Bee Bankruptcy Law, whose owner applied to participate in order to give his paralegal employee a 10% ownership interest in the business, and LawPal, which provides a platform to generate legal documents in contested and uncontested divorce and custody cases, eviction cases, and debt-related property seizure cases.

kp.k: Community health workers gain limited legal-advice roles
kp.d: Holy Cross Ministries plans to train two community health workers as bilingual medical-debt legal advocates, extending existing community services to limited-scope advice on medical debt and collateral issues. To contextualize the need, the article cites an interview with Stacy Butler reporting nearly 22,000 annual Utah lawsuits against people experiencing medical debt, a third of the state's debt-collection cases.
qs: Another participant is Holy Cross Ministries, a nonprofit organization that will train two community health workers to serve as bilingual medical-debt legal advocates.
These individuals will extend the important services they already provide within the Salt Lake City community by offering limited-scope legal advice about medical debt and collateral issues.
nearly 22,000 lawsuits are filed in Utah each year against people experiencing medical debt—a third of all debt-collection cases filed in the state.

kp.k: Evaluation examines safety, market effects, and access to justice
kp.d: IAALS identifies itself as an independent third-party evaluator through its Unlocking Legal Regulation project. Its evaluation, led by Logan Cornett, examines how the regulatory structure works and whether it achieves its goals, including consumer risk and harm, market effects, and access to justice. The intended uses are continuous improvement in Utah and informing reform elsewhere, rather than presenting a completed evaluation here.
qs: we’re analyzing data gathered from the sandbox in order to understand how the regulatory structure works in practice and whether it is achieving its intended goals.

we are looking at the entire legal landscape in Utah: the risk and harm these entities do or don’t pose to consumers, their effects on the market, and how well they can address the state’s access-to-justice crisis.
Our hope is that the evaluation findings will be used both for continuous improvement to the new regulatory structure in Utah and to inform regulatory reform efforts across the country.

kp.k: Authors advocate broader reform based on early promise
kp.d: The authors assert that the sandbox is creating jobs for lawyers and other professionals and expanding legal help. They report that more than 2,500 people received help in nine months and argue that other states should take encouragement from Utah. Their forward-looking claim is that re-regulation has potential to meaningfully increase access to justice, qualified by the need for substantially more data.
qs: creating new jobs for lawyers and other types of professionals
We still have a long way to go and a lot of data to collect, but what we’ve seen so far does suggest that re-regulation has the potential to meaningfully increase access to justice
In just nine months, more than 2,500 people have received help with housing, immigration, healthcare, discrimination, employment, and a gamut of other issues.

As more states look to re-regulation as a means to increase access to legal services, the data from Utah’s sandbox—and the real people’s lives it is impacting—should be a strong push in that direction.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cornett and DeMeola claim that Utah’s regulatory sandbox enables technology-assisted and nonlawyer-supported legal services, improves efficiency, and has the potential to expand access to justice safely.
pts.d: The source addresses regulatory reform and legal-service technology broadly, rather than making an explicit AI-specific prediction. The authors describe software delivery with lawyer involvement, chat-bots, document-generation platforms, and collaborations between lawyers and other professionals. They attribute new business possibilities to regulatory reforms and claim that instances of harm are rare and monitored. Their opening characterizes consumer-harm fears as unfounded, while their concluding assessment describes increased access to justice as a potential benefit and acknowledges that more data is needed. These are the authors’ claims, not findings about autonomous AI or measured AI performance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their claims with cumulative sandbox reporting through July 2021 and examples of participating providers.
pts.d: The September 15, 2021 article draws on the Office of Legal Services Innovation’s monthly report: 30 approved entities, over 3,000 services sought by about 2,500 unduplicated clients, and over 550 services delivered by software with lawyer involvement. It reports two harm-related complaints, one complaint per 1,000 services delivered, and one harm-related complaint per 1,500 services delivered. The authors also cite concrete provider models, including 1Law’s free and low-cost document assistance and related advice, and LawPal’s document-generation platform. The complaint-mitigation assessment is attributed to the report; the authors interpret it as suggesting remediation or prevention plans. The article does not offer a separate AI benchmark or quantified efficiency measurement.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern early sandbox activity, with continuing court-supervised regulation and evaluation; nationwide reform benefits remain prospective.
pts.d: Published September 15, 2021, the article discusses a sandbox established the previous August and cumulative reporting through July 2021. It characterizes the service-delivery period as nine months and the sandbox’s existence as just over a year. Services operate under Utah Supreme Court supervision, with risk assessments subject to ongoing adjustment. The software-delivery count expressly includes lawyer involvement. IAALS identifies itself as an independent third-party evaluator and says substantial further data collection is necessary. The authors hope future evaluation will improve Utah’s regulatory structure and inform reforms elsewhere; they give no deadline for those broader outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify benefits for consumers needing legal help, lawyers and nonlawyer professionals developing new service models, and policymakers receiving regulatory evidence.
pts.d: Consumers receive services across end-of-life planning, business matters, family law, housing, immigration, and other areas of civil legal need. Provider examples include nonlawyer ownership at 1Law, a proposed 10% ownership interest for a paralegal at Bee Bankruptcy Law, and planned training of two community health workers as bilingual medical-debt legal advocates at Holy Cross Ministries. The authors claim the sandbox creates jobs for lawyers and other professionals, without supplying a job count. Courts, policymakers, and other states are described as beneficiaries of the resulting data. These effects concern access to justice and legal-service delivery, not demonstrated AI-driven labor displacement.
